extracted.intended_audience: reading researchers, discourse analysts, journalism editors, and educators
extracted.subtask_description: Case-study analysis of how newswriting conventions (paragraphing, order of facts, connectives, etc.) affect the comprehensibility and perceived organization of newspaper narratives, with comparisons to alternative narrative organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing as discourse-structuring
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphing does not necessarily impose significant structure; the AP article uses many short paragraphs (eighteen paragraphs for 27 sentences) that do not materially improve organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat paragraphs as meaningful structural units; avoid creating many very small paragraphs that give the appearance of structure without actually helping readers reconstruct relations among facts. Anti-pattern: many subdivisions that do not map to a clear macro-organization (the AP story's 11 subdivisions for 27 sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Macrostructure: fewer, larger structural units
rubrics_metrics.description: A coherent account typically organizes material into a small number of macro-units (e.g., resume, events leading to incident, participants' accounts, authorities' accounts, consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange paragraphs so they form a reconstructable logical order and exhaust the narrative at that macro level. Example: Grant proposal / Sheila / Reporter examples are organized into 5–6 macro-units, which improves perceived organization relative to the news article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of presentation (chronological vs inverted-pyramid)
rubrics_metrics.description: The order facts are presented strongly affects comprehensibility: the AP follows the inverted-pyramid (most 'important' facts first), whereas other narratives present a brief resume then a chronological sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose ordering that matches the communicative goal and readers' needs. Anti-pattern: presenting facts in an editorially-convenient order that scatters related information and forces many reorderings for comprehension (the AP account required many reorderings to align with chronological accounts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitness of relational markers / use of connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: News accounts contain fewer connectives (words like then, because, but, as a result) than more explicitly organized narratives, making relations among facts less explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make relations among clauses and paragraphs explicit with connectives when the reader must infer causal, temporal, or logical relations. The report measures connectives per sentence and per verb to show this difference (see Table 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and irrelevance of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: In the AP account there are details that appear absolutely irrelevant to interpreting the event (e.g., the color of a scarf, exact words of an officer) which do not give the reader reason to make an inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including colorful or specific details that do not support the reader's ability to interpret the event, unless those details are explicitly tied to an interpretive claim. Anti-pattern: sprinkling apparently irrelevant 'color' that does not feed into a coherent inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundant reporting (repeating the same information in slightly different wording, e.g., multiple paraphrases of a commander's words or repeated sign wording) appears in news accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize redundancy that does not add interpretive value. If repetition is used, make explicit why the repetition matters (e.g., corroboration, contrast of accounts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of structural units relative to text length
rubrics_metrics.description: A large number of small structural units (many paragraphs or subdivisions for a short text) tends to produce a perception of disorganization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For short texts, prefer fewer, well-signposted units; excessive micro-partitioning signals lack of coherent macrostructure and hinders readers' reconstruction of relations among ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on reader inference and skimming
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard newswriting assumes readers will 'skim for facts' and co-infer relations among facts when they seem relevant; thus news style often leaves relations implicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the target reader: if readers are likely to skim, some implicitness may be acceptable; if deep comprehension is required, make connections explicit. The news structure is 'suited to the skimmer' but not to readers reconstructing event structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicative goal alignment (organization as a function of purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative organization is shaped by the narrator's perception of the discourse goal and sub-goals; different goals (academic analysis, eyewitness account, casual dinner report) produce different organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the communicative goal and choose macro-structure, ordering, and level of explicitness to serve that goal. Anti-pattern: applying newsroom editorial priorities without considering the reader's comprehension goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and placement of a brief resume/summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective narratives often open with a brief resume (summary) of the incident, then provide a detailed chronological narrative; this front-loaded summary aids reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a compact summary/resume when the reader needs an immediate grasp of the event's essentials; place detailed, chronologically ordered material afterward to support understanding and inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness vs. relevance trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who aim for 'completeness' may include many facts; but completeness without clear relevance or organization burdens reader inference and can obscure relations among facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include facts judged relevant to the account's purpose and signal their roles; avoid dumping many facts without organizing them into interpretable units or making their relevance explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and informativeness of quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Newswriting frequently includes quotations that are uninformative or do not advance understanding (e.g., stock phrases or paraphrases that add little to the facts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotations to add unique information, perspective, or to document claims; avoid including quotes that merely repeat content or provide no interpretive support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence length and variability (quantitative readability measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures such as total words, average words per sentence, and range of words per sentence affect readability; the report provides comparative numbers for AP, grant, Sheila, Reporter texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor average sentence length and variation to match genre and audience. Very long or very uniform sentence lengths can reduce comprehensibility; use these metrics diagnostically (the report compares averages and ranges across examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connectives-per-sentence and connectives-per-verb as measurable indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: The report quantifies connectives per sentence and per verb (e.g., AP .46 connectives/sentence vs Grant .83) to operationalize explicitness of relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these ratios as quantitative diagnostics of how explicitly relations are marked. Lower ratios indicate greater reliance on reader inference; higher ratios typically correlate with greater explicitness of causal/temporal/logical relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of editorial conventions for specific readers (e.g., beginning readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors' standards for beginning readers (short sentences, no paragraphing, relations implicit) have counterparts in news style but may impair developing readers' ability to expect and recognize connections among ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match editorial conventions to readers' developmental needs: for beginning readers, avoid conventions that make relations persistently implicit; explicit signaling of connections helps teach expectations about connected discourse. The report hypothesizes that exposure to texts that omit explicit relations may hinder reading development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit signaling of causal/temporal/interpretive relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives that explicitly signal causal, temporal, and interpretive relations are easier to understand than ones that leave these relations to readers' inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conjunctions, temporal adverbs, causal markers, signposting sentences and paragraph transitions to show how facts relate. Anti-pattern: listing facts without connectives or transitions, forcing heavy inferential work by the reader.
